headline: Gomakasu may come from 護摩 (goma, “a holy fire in esoteric Buddhism”) plus the suffix かす (kasu), or from 胡麻菓子 (goma kashi, “sesame candy”).

sources.quote: First recorded in the Edo period.

According to one theory, formed from 護摩 (goma, “a holy fire in esoteric Buddhism”) + verbalizing suffix かす (kasu), from a common fraud perpetrated in the Edo period of dressing as a monk and selling regular ash purported to be ash from such holy fires.
Alternatively, from 胡麻菓子 (goma kashi, “sesame candy”), from a particular sesame candy in the Edo period called 胡麻胴乱 (goma dōran) and notable for being a mostly empty shell.
The kanji spellings are examples of ateji. The more common spelling is in hiragana, as ごまかす.

headline: Kanroku originally referred to a samurai's pay, from 貫 (kan) plus 禄 (roku), the salary of someone in government service.

sources.quote: Originally referred to the (amount of) pay that a samurai in employment received and, by extension, his importance. The word consists of 貫(かん) (kan) (in its now obsolete meaning of the monetary equivalent of the income (based on crop) of a samurai) and 禄(ろく) (roku), the salary of someone in government service.
